stem: The chapter 'The Crisis of Democratic Order' deals mainly with __________.
options: The National Emergency of 1975–1977 imposed by Indira Gandhi
solution: The chapter 'The Crisis of the Democratic Order' deals mainly with the NATIONAL EMERGENCY of 1975–1977, imposed by Prime Minister Indira GANDHI. This was one of the most controversial and testing episodes in India's democratic history — a period when democratic rights and institutions were suspended. So the chapter is about the Emergency (1975–77). This is a prelims-critical topic.

stem: The National Emergency was declared in __________.
solution: The National Emergency was declared in JUNE 1975 (on 25 June 1975) by the government of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. It lasted until early 1977 (about 21 months), when it was lifted and elections were called. So the Emergency was declared in June 1975. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The Emergency was proclaimed under which constitutional provision, citing 'internal disturbance'?
solution: The Emergency was proclaimed under ARTICLE 352 of the Constitution (which provides for a NATIONAL EMERGENCY), on the ground of 'INTERNAL DISTURBANCE'. (This is distinct from Article 356, which deals with President's Rule in a state.) Under Article 352, a national emergency allows the central government to assume sweeping powers and to suspend certain fundamental rights. So the Emergency was declared under Article 352, citing internal disturbance. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: A key immediate trigger for the Emergency was the __________.
options: Allahabad High Court judgment (June 1975) that found Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractice and invalidated her election, threatening her position
solution: A key IMMEDIATE TRIGGER for the Emergency was the ALLAHABAD HIGH COURT JUDGMENT of June 1975, which found Prime Minister Indira Gandhi GUILTY of ELECTORAL MALPRACTICE (corrupt practices in her 1971 election from Rae Bareli) and INVALIDATED her election, also barring her from office for six years. This directly THREATENED her position as PM. Facing this legal blow (along with mounting political agitation demanding her resignation), her government declared the Emergency shortly afterward. So the Allahabad High Court verdict against her was a key trigger. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The mass movement against Indira Gandhi's government in 1974–75, led by Jayaprakash Narayan (JP), was known as the __________.
options: JP Movement / call for 'Total Revolution' (Sampoorna Kranti)
solution: The mass movement against Indira Gandhi's government in 1974–75 was led by the veteran socialist leader Jayaprakash NARAYAN (JP), and is known as the JP MOVEMENT. JP gave the call for 'TOTAL REVOLUTION' (Sampoorna Kranti) — a sweeping transformation of politics and society to combat corruption, misgovernance, and authoritarianism. The movement (which grew out of student agitations in Bihar and Gujarat) mobilised huge opposition to the government and demanded Indira Gandhi's resignation, forming part of the backdrop to the Emergency. So the movement was the JP Movement (Total Revolution). This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: During the Emergency, which of the following happened?
options: Fundamental rights were suspended, opposition leaders were arrested/jailed, the press was censored, and elections were postponed
The opposition was given more power
solution: During the Emergency (1975–77), the government assumed sweeping powers and democratic freedoms were curtailed: FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS were SUSPENDED (including the right to move courts to enforce them); thousands of OPPOSITION LEADERS and activists (including JP, Morarji Desai, and many others) were ARRESTED and JAILED without trial (under preventive detention laws like MISA); the PRESS was CENSORED (press freedom was suppressed); and ELECTIONS were POSTPONED (the term of the Lok Sabha was extended). Political activity and dissent were heavily restricted. So during the Emergency, rights were suspended, leaders jailed, press censored, and elections postponed. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The preventive detention law widely used to arrest opponents during the Emergency was the __________.
solution: The preventive detention law widely USED to ARREST and detain opponents (without trial) during the Emergency was MISA — the MAINTENANCE of INTERNAL SECURITY ACT. Under MISA, the government could detain people it considered a threat to internal security, and it was used to jail opposition leaders, activists, and critics during the Emergency. So the law used was MISA. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: During the Emergency, some controversial programmes were pushed, associated especially with Sanjay Gandhi. These included __________.
options: A forced sterilisation (family planning) drive and slum demolitions/'beautification'
solution: During the Emergency, some highly CONTROVERSIAL programmes were pushed — associated especially with SANJAY GANDHI (Indira Gandhi's son, who wielded great extra-constitutional power). These included a coercive FORCED STERILISATION (family planning) drive (in which many people were sterilised, often forcibly, to control population), and aggressive SLUM DEMOLITIONS and 'city BEAUTIFICATION' campaigns (which displaced many poor people, e.g., in Delhi). These excesses caused great suffering and resentment and became notorious symbols of the Emergency's abuses. So the controversial programmes included forced sterilisation and slum demolitions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Emergency is generally regarded as __________ in Indian democracy.
options: A dark period / a serious setback — when democratic rights and institutions were suppressed and power was abused
solution: The Emergency is generally regarded as a DARK PERIOD and a SERIOUS SETBACK in Indian democracy — a time when democratic RIGHTS and freedoms (speech, press, assembly, personal liberty) were SUPPRESSED, democratic INSTITUTIONS (courts, press, Parliament, the party) were undermined or subordinated, and POWER was ABUSED (mass detentions, censorship, and excesses like forced sterilisation). It stands as a cautionary episode showing how fragile democracy can be and how power can be misused. So the Emergency is regarded as a dark period/serious setback for democracy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Emergency ended when __________.
options: Indira Gandhi called fresh elections in 1977, in which her Congress was defeated
solution: The Emergency ENDED when Indira Gandhi, in early 1977, unexpectedly CALLED FRESH ELECTIONS (and released opposition leaders). In the 1977 elections, her CONGRESS was DECISIVELY DEFEATED — the electorate, angered by the Emergency's excesses, voted the Congress out of power for the FIRST TIME since independence. This brought the Emergency to an end and restored normal democratic functioning. So the Emergency ended with the 1977 elections and the Congress's defeat. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The 1977 elections resulted in __________.
options: The first non-Congress government at the centre — the Janata Party coming to power
solution: The 1977 elections resulted in the FIRST NON-CONGRESS government at the CENTRE in independent India's history. The JANATA PARTY — a coalition/merger of opposition parties (including the old Congress-O, the Jana Sangh, the Socialists, and the Bharatiya Lok Dal) that had united to fight the Emergency — came to POWER, with Morarji Desai becoming Prime Minister. This was a landmark: the peaceful, democratic removal of the Congress and the Emergency regime through the ballot box. So 1977 brought the first non-Congress (Janata Party) government at the centre. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The first non-Congress Prime Minister of India (after the 1977 elections) was __________.
solution: Morarji DESAI became the FIRST NON-CONGRESS Prime Minister of India, leading the JANATA PARTY government that came to power after the 1977 elections. His government marked the end of the Emergency and the first break in Congress rule at the centre since independence. (The Janata government, however, proved internally fractious and collapsed within a few years.) So the first non-Congress PM was Morarji Desai. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Assertion (A): The 1977 election result was a strong verdict against the Emergency. Reason (R): The people used their democratic vote to punish the government for the suspension of rights and the excesses committed during the Emergency. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the 1977 election result was a STRONG VERDICT against the EMERGENCY. And the reason is (R) that the PEOPLE used their DEMOCRATIC VOTE to PUNISH the government for the SUSPENSION of RIGHTS and the EXCESSES committed during the Emergency (mass arrests, censorship, forced sterilisation, slum demolitions). By decisively voting out the Congress — for the first time ever — the electorate expressed its rejection of the authoritarian episode. This popular anger at the Emergency's abuses directly explains the anti-Congress verdict (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: One important LESSON of the Emergency for Indian democracy was that __________.
options: Democratic institutions and the vigilance of citizens are vital, and that even a powerful government can be held accountable and removed through democratic means
solution: One important LESSON of the Emergency for Indian democracy was that DEMOCRATIC INSTITUTIONS (an independent judiciary, free press, opposition, and the rule of law) and the VIGILANCE of CITIZENS are VITAL to safeguarding freedom — their weakening allowed the abuses of the Emergency. Yet the episode ALSO showed that even a POWERFUL government can be HELD ACCOUNTABLE and REMOVED through DEMOCRATIC MEANS (the 1977 vote), demonstrating the ultimate strength of the people's democratic will. The Emergency thus reinforced the importance of protecting democratic institutions and rights against the concentration and abuse of power. So the lesson is the vitality of democratic institutions and accountability. So option 1 is correct.

stem: After the Emergency, the Constitution was amended to make it harder to impose or misuse emergency powers. This reflected __________.
options: An effort to safeguard democracy and prevent the recurrence of such abuses (e.g., the 44th Amendment introduced safeguards)
A desire to make emergencies easier
solution: After the Emergency, the Constitution was AMENDED to make it HARDER to IMPOSE or MISUSE emergency powers — reflecting an EFFORT to SAFEGUARD DEMOCRACY and PREVENT the RECURRENCE of such abuses. Notably, the 44th Amendment (1978, passed by the Janata government) introduced SAFEGUARDS: for example, changing the ground for a national emergency from 'internal disturbance' to the stricter 'ARMED REBELLION', requiring proper cabinet/parliamentary approval, and protecting certain rights (like the right to life and liberty) even during an emergency. These changes aimed to ensure emergency powers could not be abused as they had been in 1975. So the amendments reflected an effort to safeguard democracy against future misuse. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Emergency was formally proclaimed by the __________, on the advice of the Prime Minister/Cabinet.
solution: The Emergency was formally PROCLAIMED by the PRESIDENT of India (Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed was the President at the time), on the ADVICE of the Prime Minister/Cabinet — as required constitutionally. (Critics noted that the proclamation was reportedly signed hastily, before full cabinet approval, highlighting the concentration of power in the PM.) So the Emergency was formally proclaimed by the President (Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed). This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The mass movement and unrest before the Emergency had roots in __________.
options: Popular discontent over economic hardship (inflation, unemployment), corruption, and misgovernance, channelled by student agitations (in Gujarat and Bihar) and the JP movement
solution: The mass movement and unrest before the Emergency had roots in widespread POPULAR DISCONTENT: ECONOMIC HARDSHIP (high INFLATION and rising prices, UNEMPLOYMENT, shortages, worsened by the oil crisis and the costs of the 1971 war), and anger over CORRUPTION and MISGOVERNANCE. This discontent was CHANNELLED by STUDENT AGITATIONS — first the Nav Nirman movement in GUJARAT and then a major student movement in BIHAR — which grew into the broader JP MOVEMENT (Total Revolution) led by Jayaprakash Narayan, mounting a powerful challenge to Indira Gandhi's government. So the unrest was rooted in economic hardship, corruption, and misgovernance, channelled by the student/JP agitations. So option 1 is correct.

stem: During the Emergency, the government also carried out a controversial constitutional amendment. The 42nd Amendment (1976) __________.
options: Made wide-ranging changes that increased the power of the central government/Parliament and curtailed the judiciary and rights (it was later partly reversed)
solution: During the Emergency, the government pushed through the controversial 42nd CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT (1976), often called a 'mini-constitution' for its sweeping scope. It made WIDE-RANGING CHANGES that INCREASED the POWER of the central government and Parliament, CURTAILED the JUDICIARY (limiting judicial review) and civil liberties, extended the terms of legislatures, and added the words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to the Preamble, among other changes. Many of its provisions were seen as tilting the balance dangerously toward the executive/Parliament and away from checks and rights. It was LATER PARTLY REVERSED (notably by the 44th Amendment) after the Emergency. So the 42nd Amendment made sweeping pro-government changes, later partly reversed. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Shah Commission was set up after the Emergency to __________.
options: Inquire into the excesses and abuses committed during the Emergency
solution: The SHAH COMMISSION was set up by the Janata government (after the Emergency ended) to INQUIRE into the EXCESSES and ABUSES committed during the EMERGENCY (1975–77). Headed by Justice J.C. Shah, the Commission investigated the various irregularities, illegal detentions, misuse of power, censorship, and coercive actions (like the forced sterilisations) of the Emergency period, and documented them in its reports. It was an effort to establish accountability for what had happened. So the Shah Commission inquired into the Emergency's excesses. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Assertion (A): The Emergency revealed weaknesses in India's institutional checks on executive power. Reason (R): Institutions like Parliament, the judiciary, and the press largely failed to effectively restrain the government's actions during the Emergency. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Emergency REVEALED WEAKNESSES in India's INSTITUTIONAL CHECKS on EXECUTIVE POWER. And the reason is (R) that institutions meant to restrain the government — PARLIAMENT (dominated by the ruling party, it approved the Emergency and the 42nd Amendment), the JUDICIARY (which, in the controversial ADM Jabalpur case, upheld the suspension of even the right to life/liberty), and the PRESS (which was CENSORED into silence) — LARGELY FAILED to EFFECTIVELY RESTRAIN the government's actions during the Emergency. This failure of the checking institutions is precisely what exposed the weaknesses in the system's safeguards (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The Emergency period saw the rise to prominence of __________, who wielded great extra-constitutional power.
solution: The Emergency period saw the rise to prominence of SANJAY GANDHI, Indira Gandhi's younger son, who — though holding no formal government office — wielded enormous EXTRA-CONSTITUTIONAL POWER and influence. He was the driving force behind several of the Emergency's most notorious programmes (like the forced sterilisation drive and the slum demolitions), and his unaccountable exercise of power symbolised the arbitrariness of the period. So Sanjay Gandhi rose to prominence with great extra-constitutional power. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Which of the following best captures the debate about whether the Emergency was justified?
options: The government claimed it was needed to restore order and stability amid the agitations; critics argued it was an unjustified, self-serving suppression of democracy to protect Indira Gandhi's power
solution: The debate about whether the Emergency was JUSTIFIED has two sides. The GOVERNMENT (Indira Gandhi's side) CLAIMED it was NEEDED to RESTORE ORDER and STABILITY amid the widespread AGITATIONS (the JP movement), which it portrayed as a threat to the country and to democratically elected authority. CRITICS, however, argued that the Emergency was an UNJUSTIFIED, SELF-SERVING SUPPRESSION of DEMOCRACY — that its real purpose was to PROTECT Indira Gandhi's POWER (after the court verdict against her) by silencing opposition, and that the 'threat' was exaggerated and the response grossly disproportionate and abusive. Most assessments side with the critics, viewing the Emergency as an abuse of power. So the debate is between the government's order-and-stability claim and the critics' view of it as unjustified suppression. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 1977 election and the peaceful transfer of power to the Janata Party demonstrated __________.
options: The deep roots and resilience of Indian democracy — that the people could reject authoritarianism and that power could change hands peacefully even after the Emergency
solution: The 1977 ELECTION and the PEACEFUL TRANSFER of power to the JANATA PARTY demonstrated the DEEP ROOTS and RESILIENCE of Indian DEMOCRACY. Despite the authoritarian interlude of the Emergency, the PEOPLE — given the chance to vote — REJECTED authoritarianism, voting the Congress out of power; and the government ACCEPTED the verdict, allowing POWER to CHANGE HANDS PEACEFULLY to the opposition. This showed that India's commitment to democracy ran deep among its people and that the democratic system could recover and reassert itself even after being suspended. So it demonstrated the deep roots and resilience of Indian democracy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Janata Party government (1977–79), though it ended the Emergency era, __________.
options: Proved internally divided and unstable, and collapsed within a few years due to infighting, leading to the Congress's return in 1980
solution: The JANATA PARTY government (1977–79), though it ended the Emergency era and restored democracy, PROVED INTERNALLY DIVIDED and UNSTABLE. Being a hastily assembled coalition/merger of very different parties and ambitious leaders (with clashing ideologies and personal rivalries), it was plagued by INFIGHTING and power struggles, and it COLLAPSED within a few years. This led to fresh elections and the RETURN of Indira Gandhi's CONGRESS to power in 1980. The Janata experience illustrated the difficulties of holding together an ideologically disparate coalition. So the Janata government was unstable and collapsed, leading to the Congress's return in 1980. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The lasting significance of the Emergency in Indian political memory is that it __________.
options: Serves as a stark warning about the fragility of democracy and the dangers of concentrated, unchecked power, reinforcing public commitment to democratic rights and institutions
solution: The LASTING SIGNIFICANCE of the Emergency in Indian political memory is that it serves as a STARK WARNING about the FRAGILITY of DEMOCRACY and the DANGERS of CONCENTRATED, UNCHECKED POWER — showing how quickly rights and freedoms can be suspended and institutions subverted when power is abused. Precisely because of this traumatic experience, the Emergency REINFORCED public and political COMMITMENT to protecting DEMOCRATIC RIGHTS, civil liberties, the rule of law, and independent INSTITUTIONS. It remains a powerful reference point and cautionary tale in India's democratic consciousness. So its lasting significance is as a warning that strengthens commitment to democracy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In conclusion, the Emergency episode shows that Indian democracy __________.
options: Was tested to its limits but ultimately survived and recovered, emerging with a renewed appreciation of the value of democratic institutions, rights, and accountability
solution: In conclusion, the Emergency episode shows that Indian DEMOCRACY was TESTED to its LIMITS — its rights suspended, its institutions subverted, and its very survival in doubt — but that it ULTIMATELY SURVIVED and RECOVERED. Through the people's decisive rejection of authoritarianism in the 1977 election and the peaceful restoration of democratic government, India emerged from the crisis with a RENEWED APPRECIATION of the VALUE of democratic INSTITUTIONS, civil RIGHTS, and ACCOUNTABILITY — and with new safeguards to guard against future abuse. The Emergency thus stands as both a grave crisis and a testament to the resilience of Indian democracy. So Indian democracy was tested but survived and recovered, with renewed appreciation for democratic values. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The student movement in Gujarat in 1973–74 that protested against corruption and price rise, and contributed to the pre-Emergency ferment, was the __________.
solution: The NAV NIRMAN ANDOLAN (Nav Nirman Movement) was a student-led protest in GUJARAT in 1973–74 against CORRUPTION, mismanagement, and rising PRICES (and the state government). It succeeded in forcing the dismissal of the state government and fresh elections, and it INSPIRED and contributed to the wider PRE-EMERGENCY FERMENT (including the Bihar movement and the JP movement). So the Gujarat student movement was the Nav Nirman Andolan. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Jayaprakash Narayan (JP), the leader of the anti-Emergency movement, was a veteran __________.
options: Freedom fighter and socialist leader (a Gandhian who had been part of the independence struggle)
solution: Jayaprakash NARAYAN (JP) was a VETERAN FREEDOM FIGHTER and SOCIALIST LEADER — a Gandhian and one of the heroes of the independence struggle (famous for his role in the 1942 Quit India Movement) who had later devoted himself to socialist and Sarvodaya (social service) work. His immense moral stature and clean image made him the natural leader of the popular movement against Indira Gandhi's government in 1974–75 (the call for 'Total Revolution'). He was jailed during the Emergency. So JP was a veteran freedom fighter and socialist leader. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: During the Emergency, the fundamental right that was suspended included even the right to move courts for __________.
options: Enforcement of fundamental rights (including, controversially, habeas corpus / the right to life and liberty)
solution: During the Emergency, the government suspended the citizens' right to move the COURTS for the ENFORCEMENT of FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS. Most controversially, in the ADM Jabalpur case (the 'Habeas Corpus case', 1976), the Supreme Court held that even the right to move courts for HABEAS CORPUS — to challenge unlawful detention, i.e., the RIGHT to LIFE and personal LIBERTY (Article 21) — stood suspended during the Emergency. This meant detained persons had NO legal remedy against even illegal imprisonment — a deeply criticised outcome that highlighted the collapse of legal safeguards. So even the right to enforce fundamental rights (including habeas corpus/life and liberty) was suspended. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The censorship of the press during the Emergency meant that __________.
options: Newspapers had to submit content for prior government approval, news critical of the government was suppressed, and press freedom was effectively muzzled
The press supported the opposition openly
solution: The CENSORSHIP of the PRESS during the Emergency meant that newspapers were subjected to PRIOR RESTRAINT — often having to SUBMIT their content for GOVERNMENT APPROVAL before publication — and that NEWS and comment CRITICAL of the government were SUPPRESSED. Press FREEDOM was effectively MUZZLED: critical journalists faced pressure, some publications resisted (famously, a few printed blank editorials in protest), and the flow of independent information was choked. This silencing of the press was one of the most serious assaults on democratic freedoms during the Emergency. So censorship meant prior approval, suppression of criticism, and muzzling of the press. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The forced sterilisation drive during the Emergency was especially resented because __________.
options: People were often coerced or compelled into sterilisation (against their will), and officials pursued targets ruthlessly, causing fear, abuse, and suffering, especially among the poor
It was entirely voluntary and welcomed
It had no impact on people
solution: The FORCED STERILISATION drive during the Emergency (part of the family-planning programme, pushed aggressively by Sanjay Gandhi) was especially RESENTED because people were often COERCED or COMPELLED into sterilisation AGAINST their WILL — officials, under pressure to meet sterilisation TARGETS, pursued them RUTHLESSLY, sometimes rounding up men (including the unmarried or elderly) and using threats or force. This caused widespread FEAR, ABUSE, humiliation, and SUFFERING, falling especially hard on the POOR and vulnerable. The programme became one of the most hated symbols of the Emergency's excesses and turned many people against the government. So it was resented because of coercion, ruthless targets, and abuse of the poor. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The 44th Amendment (1978) changed the ground for declaring a national emergency. Reason (R): It replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' to make it harder to misuse the emergency provision as had happened in 1975. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the 44th AMENDMENT (1978) CHANGED the GROUND for declaring a national emergency. And the reason is (R) that it REPLACED the vague, easily invoked term 'INTERNAL DISTURBANCE' with the much narrower and more serious 'ARMED REBELLION' — precisely to make it HARDER to MISUSE the emergency provision (under Article 352) as had happened in 1975, when 'internal disturbance' had been used to justify the Emergency. This tightening of the ground was a deliberate safeguard against a repeat abuse (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The role of the courts (judiciary) during and after the Emergency shows that __________.
options: The judiciary largely failed to protect rights during the Emergency (e.g., the Habeas Corpus case), but the experience later spurred a more assertive judicial defence of rights and the basic structure of the Constitution
The judiciary always perfectly protected rights
solution: The role of the COURTS shows a two-part story. DURING the Emergency, the judiciary LARGELY FAILED to protect citizens' rights — most notoriously in the ADM Jabalpur/HABEAS CORPUS case (1976), where the Supreme Court held that even the right to life and liberty could be suspended, leaving detainees without remedy. However, the traumatic EXPERIENCE of the Emergency LATER SPURRED a MORE ASSERTIVE JUDICIARY — one more determined to DEFEND fundamental RIGHTS, judicial review, and the 'BASIC STRUCTURE' of the Constitution (a doctrine that limits even Parliament's power to amend the Constitution's core features) against future encroachment. So the judiciary largely failed during the Emergency but became more protective of rights afterward. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Emergency had important effects on the party system, including __________.
options: The coming together of opposition parties (which merged to form the Janata Party) and the eventual strengthening of non-Congress alternatives in Indian politics
The banning of all parties forever
The permanent dominance of the Congress
solution: The Emergency had important EFFECTS on the PARTY SYSTEM. Above all, the shared experience of opposing the Emergency brought the diverse OPPOSITION PARTIES TOGETHER — they MERGED to form the JANATA PARTY, which defeated the Congress in 1977. Although the Janata experiment soon collapsed, the episode marked a crucial step in the STRENGTHENING of NON-CONGRESS ALTERNATIVES in Indian politics: it broke the Congress's aura of invincibility, gave opposition forces (including the Jana Sangh element, later the BJP) national governing experience, and accelerated the long-term move toward a more competitive, multi-party system. So the Emergency spurred opposition unity (the Janata Party) and strengthened non-Congress alternatives. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly sequences the Emergency-related events?
options: JP movement (1974–75) → Allahabad HC verdict (June 1975) → Emergency declared (25 June 1975) → 1977 elections → Congress defeated, Janata government
Emergency declared → JP movement → Allahabad verdict → Janata government
1977 elections → Emergency declared → JP movement → Allahabad verdict
Janata government → Emergency → JP movement → 1977 elections
solution: The correct sequence is: the JP MOVEMENT (Total Revolution) gathering force in 1974–75 → the ALLAHABAD HIGH COURT VERDICT invalidating Indira Gandhi's election (June 1975) → the EMERGENCY DECLARED (25 June 1975) → (after ~21 months) the 1977 ELECTIONS → the CONGRESS DEFEATED and the JANATA government coming to power. Knowing this chronological sequence is prelims-relevant. So option 1 gives the correct order. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Emergency raised the fundamental question of __________.
options: The balance between the government's need for order/stability and the citizens' democratic rights and freedoms — and where the limits of governmental power should lie
solution: The Emergency raised the FUNDAMENTAL QUESTION of the BALANCE between the government's claimed need for ORDER and STABILITY (its justification for the Emergency) and the CITIZENS' democratic RIGHTS and FREEDOMS — and, crucially, of WHERE the LIMITS of GOVERNMENTAL POWER should lie in a democracy. It forced a national reckoning with how far a government may go in the name of stability or security before it destroys the very democracy it claims to protect, and how to safeguard rights and institutions against such overreach. So the Emergency raised the question of balancing governmental power/order against democratic rights. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The Emergency ultimately strengthened Indians' commitment to democracy. Reason (R): The bitter experience of losing their freedoms made people value democratic rights more and become more vigilant against authoritarianism. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Emergency ULTIMATELY STRENGTHENED Indians' COMMITMENT to DEMOCRACY. And the reason is (R) that the BITTER EXPERIENCE of LOSING their FREEDOMS (rights suspended, dissent crushed, excesses committed) made people VALUE democratic RIGHTS more deeply and become more VIGILANT against AUTHORITARIANISM — as they demonstrated by voting out the government in 1977. Having tasted the loss of liberty, citizens came to cherish and guard it more firmly. This experience-driven deepening of democratic commitment is precisely how the Emergency strengthened it (A). So R correctly explains A. (A rare case where a threat to democracy ended up reinforcing it.)

stem: The Emergency is a key case study in Indian democracy because it __________.
options: Illustrates both the vulnerabilities of a democracy (how rights and institutions can be suspended) and its capacity for self-correction (through elections and the people's will)
Shows democracy can never be threatened
solution: The Emergency is a key CASE STUDY in Indian democracy because it ILLUSTRATES BOTH sides of the democratic experience: on one hand, the VULNERABILITIES of a democracy — how, under a determined and powerful leader, democratic RIGHTS and INSTITUTIONS can be SUSPENDED, checks bypassed, and power abused; and on the other hand, the capacity for SELF-CORRECTION — how the system, through ELECTIONS and the PEOPLE's WILL, can REJECT authoritarianism and RESTORE democratic government. Studying the Emergency thus teaches both the fragility and the resilience of democracy, and the importance of safeguarding it. So it illustrates both democracy's vulnerabilities and its capacity for self-correction. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The government's official justification for the Emergency emphasised __________.
options: The threat to law, order, and stability posed by the agitations, and the need to ensure discipline and continue development
The desire to abolish democracy openly
The need to help the opposition
solution: The government's OFFICIAL JUSTIFICATION for the Emergency emphasised the alleged THREAT to LAW, ORDER, and STABILITY posed by the widespread AGITATIONS (the JP movement, strikes, and unrest) — which it characterised as a threat to the country and to democratically constituted authority — and the NEED to ensure DISCIPLINE, restore stability, and CONTINUE DEVELOPMENT and economic progress (a '20-point programme' was announced). Critics, of course, disputed this justification as a pretext for suppressing legitimate dissent and protecting Indira Gandhi's power. So the official justification stressed order, stability, discipline, and development. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The most important takeaway from the Emergency for protecting democracy is that __________.
options: Strong, independent institutions (judiciary, press, election commission), an active civil society, and constitutional safeguards are essential checks on the abuse of power
Concentrating all power in one leader is safe
The people should not participate in politics
solution: The most important TAKEAWAY from the Emergency for PROTECTING DEMOCRACY is that STRONG, INDEPENDENT INSTITUTIONS — an independent JUDICIARY, a free PRESS, an impartial ELECTION COMMISSION, and a robust Parliament — together with an ACTIVE CIVIL SOCIETY (alert citizens, opposition, and public opinion) and firm CONSTITUTIONAL SAFEGUARDS, are ESSENTIAL CHECKS on the ABUSE of POWER. The Emergency happened partly because these checks were weak or subverted; preventing a recurrence requires keeping them strong and vigilant. This is the enduring lesson. So the takeaway is the essential role of strong institutions, civil society, and safeguards. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Congress's defeat in 1977 was especially significant because it was the __________.
options: First time the Congress had lost power at the centre since independence (1947), ending three decades of Congress rule
solution: The Congress's defeat in the 1977 elections was especially SIGNIFICANT because it was the FIRST TIME the Congress had LOST POWER at the CENTRE since independence in 1947 — ending nearly THREE DECADES of continuous Congress rule at the national level. This historic first alternation of power (to the Janata Party) demonstrated that no party was permanently entrenched and that the Indian electorate could decisively change its government through the ballot, even after an authoritarian interlude. So the 1977 defeat was the Congress's first loss of central power since independence. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter's discussion of the Emergency is relevant today because it __________.
options: Reminds citizens and leaders of the importance of upholding democratic values, rights, and institutional checks, and of remaining vigilant against the misuse of power
Concerns only the distant past with no present relevance
solution: The chapter's discussion of the Emergency is RELEVANT TODAY because it REMINDS both CITIZENS and LEADERS of the enduring importance of UPHOLDING DEMOCRATIC VALUES, RIGHTS, and INSTITUTIONAL CHECKS and balances, and of remaining VIGILANT against the MISUSE and over-concentration of POWER. The Emergency stands as a permanent cautionary lesson about how democracy can be endangered from within, and about the need to protect civil liberties, the rule of law, and independent institutions — concerns that remain vital in any era. So the Emergency's lessons about vigilance and democratic values remain relevant today. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In summary, 'The Crisis of the Democratic Order' teaches that __________.
options: Democracy is precious but not automatically secure — it must be actively defended through strong institutions, protected rights, and vigilant citizens, as the Emergency and India's recovery from it demonstrate
solution: In summary, 'The Crisis of the Democratic Order' teaches that DEMOCRACY is PRECIOUS but NOT AUTOMATICALLY SECURE — it can be endangered and suspended, as the EMERGENCY showed. Therefore it must be ACTIVELY DEFENDED — through STRONG, independent INSTITUTIONS, firmly PROTECTED RIGHTS and constitutional safeguards, and VIGILANT, engaged CITIZENS willing to resist and reverse the abuse of power. India's descent into the Emergency AND its RECOVERY from it (through the people's democratic verdict in 1977) together demonstrate both the fragility and the resilience of democracy, and the ongoing responsibility to safeguard it. So the chapter teaches that democracy must be actively defended. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The imposition of the Emergency showed how __________ can be used (and misused) within a constitutional democracy.
options: Legal and constitutional provisions (like emergency powers) themselves
solution: A striking and sobering feature of the Emergency is that it was imposed NOT through a military coup or the open overthrow of the Constitution, but by USING the LEGAL and CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS themselves — specifically the EMERGENCY POWERS (Article 352) that the Constitution provided. This showed how such provisions, though designed for genuine crises, can be MISUSED by those in power to legally suspend rights and concentrate authority WITHIN a constitutional democracy. It highlighted that legal-constitutional tools are not self-protecting and can be abused, underscoring the need for careful safeguards (later added by the 44th Amendment). So the Emergency showed how constitutional/legal provisions themselves can be used and misused. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Bihar movement, an important part of the pre-Emergency agitation, was led/guided by __________.
options: Jayaprakash Narayan (JP), who took charge of the student-led movement and broadened it
solution: The BIHAR MOVEMENT (a major student-led agitation in Bihar in 1974 against corruption, misgovernment, and price rise) was led and GUIDED by Jayaprakash NARAYAN (JP), who was invited to take charge of it. JP BROADENED the movement from a student protest into a wider political struggle, giving the call for 'Total Revolution' and demanding sweeping change and, eventually, Indira Gandhi's resignation. The Bihar movement, along with the Gujarat Nav Nirman movement, was a key part of the mass ferment that preceded the Emergency. So the Bihar movement was led by JP. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Assertion (A): The Emergency concentrated power in the hands of the Prime Minister and a small coterie. Reason (R): With rights suspended, opposition jailed, press censored, and institutions subdued, there were few effective checks on the executive during this period. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Emergency CONCENTRATED POWER in the hands of the PRIME MINISTER (Indira Gandhi) and a small coterie (including Sanjay Gandhi and close aides). And the reason is (R) that WITH fundamental RIGHTS SUSPENDED, the OPPOSITION JAILED, the PRESS CENSORED, and other INSTITUTIONS (Parliament, courts) SUBDUED, there were FEW EFFECTIVE CHECKS on the EXECUTIVE during this period. The removal or neutralisation of all the normal restraints on power directly enabled and reflected its concentration in a few hands (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The most lasting positive outcome of the Emergency crisis was arguably __________.
options: The reaffirmation, by the people and the system, that India would remain a democracy — and the reinforcement of safeguards and civic vigilance to protect it
solution: The most LASTING POSITIVE OUTCOME of the Emergency crisis was arguably the REAFFIRMATION — by the PEOPLE (through the 1977 vote) and by the SYSTEM (through the restoration of democratic government and new safeguards) — that INDIA would REMAIN a DEMOCRACY. Out of a grave threat, India emerged with its democratic commitment renewed and strengthened: with reinforced constitutional SAFEGUARDS (like the 44th Amendment), a more assertive judiciary and press, and heightened CIVIC VIGILANCE to protect democracy against future abuse. This democratic reaffirmation and strengthening of safeguards was the crisis's silver lining. So the lasting positive outcome was the reaffirmation and safeguarding of democracy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall significance of studying the Emergency is that it __________.
options: Helps us understand a critical test of Indian democracy, the dangers of unchecked power, and the resilience and value of democratic institutions and rights
solution: The overall SIGNIFICANCE of studying the Emergency is that it HELPS US UNDERSTAND: a CRITICAL TEST of Indian DEMOCRACY (its gravest internal challenge); the DANGERS of UNCHECKED, concentrated POWER and the abuse of authority; and, crucially, the RESILIENCE and VALUE of democratic INSTITUTIONS, RIGHTS, and the people's democratic will (which ultimately reversed the crisis). It offers profound lessons about how democracies can be endangered and how they can recover, making it essential for understanding both India's political history and the enduring requirements of a healthy democracy. So studying it illuminates a key test of democracy and the dangers of unchecked power. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In conclusion, the Emergency and the return to democracy in 1977 together demonstrate that __________.
options: Indian democracy, though it can be gravely threatened, ultimately rests on the sovereignty of the people, who can and did reclaim their democratic rights
Democracy in India is a myth
Only leaders matter, not the people
solution: In conclusion, the EMERGENCY and the RETURN to DEMOCRACY in 1977 together demonstrate that INDIAN DEMOCRACY — though it CAN be GRAVELY THREATENED and even suspended — ULTIMATELY RESTS on the SOVEREIGNTY of the PEOPLE. It was the PEOPLE who, when finally given the chance to vote in 1977, DECISIVELY REJECTED authoritarianism and RECLAIMED their DEMOCRATIC RIGHTS, restoring democratic government. This affirms the foundational democratic principle that ultimate power lies with the citizens, and that a determined people can defend and recover their freedom. So the episode demonstrates that Indian democracy rests on the sovereignty of the people, who reclaimed their rights. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The chapter 'The Crisis of Democratic Order' deals mainly with the __________ of 1975–77.
solution: The chapter deals mainly with the National Emergency of 1975–77 and the surrounding events.

stem: The National Emergency was declared in the year:
solution: The National Emergency was declared in June 1975.

stem: The Emergency was proclaimed under the constitutional provision (Article 352) citing:
solution: The 1975 Emergency was proclaimed under Article 352 on the ground of 'internal disturbance'.

stem: A key immediate trigger for the Emergency was the:
options: Allahabad High Court verdict setting aside Indira Gandhi's election (and the mounting opposition movement)
solution: The immediate trigger was the Allahabad High Court judgment invalidating Indira Gandhi's election, combined with the mounting opposition movement.

stem: The Allahabad High Court judgment of 1975 against Indira Gandhi:
options: found her guilty of electoral malpractice and declared her election invalid
solution: The Allahabad High Court found Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractices and declared her Lok Sabha election invalid.

stem: The mass movement against Indira Gandhi's government in 1974–75, led by Jayaprakash Narayan (JP), was known as the:
solution: The anti-government movement led by JP was known as the JP Movement, and JP called for a 'Total Revolution'.

stem: Jayaprakash Narayan (JP), the leader of the anti-Emergency movement, was a veteran:
solution: Jayaprakash Narayan was a veteran freedom fighter and socialist leader who led the movement against the Emergency.

stem: The student movement in Gujarat in 1973–74, protesting against corruption and price rise, was the:
solution: The Nav Nirman Movement in Gujarat (1973–74) protested against corruption and price rise, contributing to the pre-Emergency ferment.

stem: The Bihar movement, an important part of the pre-Emergency agitation, was led/guided by:
solution: The Bihar movement of 1974 was led/guided by Jayaprakash Narayan, becoming a focal point of the anti-government agitation.

stem: The preventive detention law widely used to arrest opponents during the Emergency was the:
solution: The Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA) was widely used for preventive detention of opponents during the Emergency.

stem: During the Emergency, the fundamental right that was suspended included even the right to move the courts for:
options: the enforcement of fundamental rights (habeas corpus)
solution: During the Emergency, even the right to move courts for the enforcement of fundamental rights (including habeas corpus) was suspended.

stem: The censorship of the press during the Emergency meant that:
options: newspapers were subjected to prior censorship and could not freely criticise the government
the press supported the opposition freely
solution: Press censorship meant newspapers faced prior restraint and could not freely report or criticise the government during the Emergency.

stem: During the Emergency, controversial programmes associated especially with Sanjay Gandhi included:
options: forced sterilisation and slum demolition drives
solution: Programmes associated with Sanjay Gandhi included coercive family-planning (forced sterilisation) and slum-clearance/demolition drives.

stem: The forced sterilisation drive during the Emergency was especially resented because:
options: people were coerced into sterilisation, often through excesses and abuse of power
solution: The sterilisation drive was resented because people were coerced, with widespread excesses and abuse of official power.

stem: The 42nd Amendment (1976), passed during the Emergency:
options: made sweeping changes curtailing the courts' powers and enhancing Parliament's/executive's power
solution: The 42nd Amendment made sweeping changes that curtailed the courts' powers and increased the power of the executive/Parliament.

stem: The government's official justification for the Emergency emphasised:
options: the need to restore order, discipline and stability amid threats of internal disturbance
solution: The government justified the Emergency as necessary to restore order, discipline and stability in the face of threats to internal security.

stem: The Emergency ended when:
options: Indira Gandhi called fresh elections in 1977, which her party lost
solution: The Emergency effectively ended when Indira Gandhi called fresh elections in early 1977, which her party lost.

stem: The 1977 elections resulted in:
options: the defeat of the Congress and the victory of the Janata Party
a hung parliament with Congress leading
solution: In the 1977 elections the Congress was defeated and the Janata Party came to power.

stem: The first non-Congress Prime Minister of India (after the 1977 elections) was:
solution: Morarji Desai, of the Janata Party, became India's first non-Congress Prime Minister in 1977.

stem: The Congress's defeat in 1977 was especially significant because it was the:
options: first time it had ever won
first time the Congress had been voted out of power at the centre since independence
solution: The 1977 defeat was significant as the first time the Congress had been voted out of power at the national level since independence.

stem: The Shah Commission was set up after the Emergency to:
options: inquire into the excesses and abuses committed during the Emergency
solution: The Shah Commission was appointed to investigate the excesses and abuses of power committed during the Emergency.

stem: The 44th Amendment (1978) changed the ground for declaring a national emergency by:
options: replacing 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' (to make misuse harder)
solution: The 44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion', adding safeguards to prevent misuse of the emergency provision.

stem: After the Emergency, the constitutional amendments (like the 44th) to make emergency powers harder to misuse reflected:
options: a determination to safeguard democracy and prevent a repeat of the Emergency
solution: Post-Emergency amendments reflected a determination to safeguard democratic rights and prevent any future misuse of emergency powers.

stem: The Janata Party government (1977–79), though it ended the Emergency era:
options: was short-lived, collapsing due to internal conflicts and lack of cohesion
solution: The Janata Party government was short-lived, collapsing by 1979 due to internal conflicts and lack of cohesion among its constituents.

stem: The Emergency had important effects on the party system, including:

solution: The Emergency spurred opposition parties to unite; several merged to form the Janata Party, which defeated the Congress in 1977.

stem: The Emergency raised the fundamental question of:
options: the balance between the government's authority and citizens' rights, and the safeguards needed against the abuse of power
solution: The Emergency raised the fundamental question of balancing governmental authority with citizens' rights, and of the safeguards needed against abuse of power.

stem: The role of the courts (judiciary) during and after the Emergency shows that:

solution: The judiciary largely failed to check the executive during the Emergency but reasserted its role afterwards — showing both its vulnerability and its importance.

stem: The 1977 election and the peaceful transfer of power to the Janata Party demonstrated:

solution: The 1977 election and peaceful transfer of power showed the resilience of Indian democracy — the people used the ballot to restore democratic order.

stem: An important LESSON of the Emergency was that:

the executive should have unlimited power

stem: The lasting significance of the Emergency in Indian political memory is that it:

solution: The Emergency remains a powerful warning against authoritarianism and reinforced Indians' commitment to democratic rights and vigilance.

stem: The most lasting positive outcome of the Emergency crisis was arguably:

stem: The chapter's discussion of the Emergency is relevant today because it:

stem: The overall significance of studying the Emergency is that it:

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter 'The Crisis of Democratic Order'?
options: The Emergency strengthened democracy from the start

The Emergency (1975–77) was a grave crisis in which democratic rights were suspended and power abused, but the 1977 restoration of democracy showed the resilience of Indian democracy and the importance of safeguarding rights
the Emergency was a minor event
solution: The chapter concludes that the Emergency was a grave crisis of suspended rights and abused power, but the 1977 restoration of democracy revealed the resilience of Indian democracy and underscored the need to safeguard democratic rights and institutions.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'The Crisis of Democratic Order' is that:
options: The NATIONAL EMERGENCY of 1975–77 (declared by Indira Gandhi under Article 352 on the ground of 'internal disturbance', in the context of the Allahabad High Court verdict against her and the JP-led mass movement) was a grave CRISIS for Indian democracy — during which fundamental rights were suspended, thousands of opposition leaders were jailed (under laws like MISA), the press was censored, elections were postponed, and there were serious abuses (like forced sterilisation and slum demolitions, associated with Sanjay Gandhi); but Indian democracy ultimately proved resilient — the Emergency was ended when Indira Gandhi called elections in 1977, in which the Congress was decisively defeated and the first non-Congress (Janata Party) government came to power, and the episode led to safeguards (like the 44th Amendment) and left an enduring lesson about the importance of protecting democratic institutions, rights, and the rule of law against the abuse of power
The Emergency had no effect on India
Democracy was permanently destroyed by the Emergency
solution: The chapter's overall message is that the NATIONAL EMERGENCY of 1975–1977 was a GRAVE CRISIS — indeed a testing point — for INDIAN DEMOCRACY. It was declared by Prime Minister Indira GANDHI in June 1975 under ARTICLE 352 (on the ground of 'INTERNAL DISTURBANCE'), in the context of the ALLAHABAD HIGH COURT verdict that had invalidated her election and the massive JP-led MASS MOVEMENT (the call for 'Total Revolution') demanding her resignation. During the Emergency, DEMOCRATIC RIGHTS and institutions were SUPPRESSED: FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS were suspended; thousands of OPPOSITION leaders and activists were JAILED without trial (under MISA); the PRESS was CENSORED; ELECTIONS were postponed; and there were serious ABUSES and excesses — notably the coercive FORCED STERILISATION drive and SLUM DEMOLITIONS associated with SANJAY GANDHI — that caused great suffering and resentment. Yet Indian democracy ultimately proved RESILIENT: the Emergency was ENDED when Indira Gandhi called fresh ELECTIONS in 1977, in which the CONGRESS was DECISIVELY DEFEATED (for the first time since independence) and the first NON-CONGRESS government — the JANATA PARTY, under Morarji Desai — came to power, demonstrating the people's power to hold even a mighty government accountable through the ballot. The episode also led to constitutional SAFEGUARDS (like the 44th AMENDMENT, making emergency powers harder to misuse) and left an ENDURING LESSON about the vital importance of PROTECTING democratic INSTITUTIONS, RIGHTS, and the RULE of LAW against the concentration and ABUSE of POWER. So the overall message is option 2.
